title: OSI vs TCP/IP Reference Models
summary: Understand why networks are built in layers, and translate confidently between the OSI 7-layer teaching model and the TCP/IP 4-layer model the internet actually runs.

slides.markdown:
Every network conversation gets broken into **layers**, each solving one problem and handing a clean interface to the layer above it. The classic teaching model is **OSI** (7 layers); the model the real internet runs on is **TCP/IP** (4 layers).

Think of a postal system: you write a letter (application), someone seals it in an addressed envelope (transport/network), and a courier moves the envelope without ever reading the letter inside (link). Each layer only needs to understand its own job.

slides.subTitle: Separating concerns
slides.markdown:
Layering exists to **separate concerns**: a change to how Wi-Fi encodes bits shouldn't force you to rewrite your browser, and a new app protocol shouldn't require redesigning Ethernet. Each layer exposes a fixed interface upward and hides its own implementation below.

That's why HTTP works identically over Wi-Fi, fiber, or a cellular link — the application layer never has to know which one is carrying its bytes. You can swap one layer's technology (IPv4 → IPv6, copper → fiber) without touching the others, as long as the interface contract holds.

**OSI** stacks seven layers, bits at the bottom and user-facing meaning at the top. Each layer only talks to the ones directly above and below it.

![OSI seven layers stacked from Physical to Application](assets/osi-seven-layers.svg)

Mnemonic aside, what matters for interviews is knowing which real protocols sit where — HTTP at 7, TCP/UDP at 4, IP at 3, Ethernet at 2.

assets.alt: OSI seven layers stacked from Physical to Application

slides.markdown:
The internet doesn't run OSI — it runs **TCP/IP**, which merges OSI's top three layers into one **Application** layer and its bottom two into one **Link** layer.

![TCP/IP four layers: Application, Transport, Internet, Link](assets/tcpip-four-layers.svg)

TCP/IP won because it shipped as working code on the early ARPANET while OSI was still a committee spec — a good lesson in "working beats perfect."

assets.alt: TCP/IP four layers: Application, Transport, Internet, Link

slides.markdown:
| TCP/IP layer | OSI layers it absorbs | Example protocols |
|---|---|---|
| Application | 7 Application, 6 Presentation, 5 Session | HTTP, DNS, TLS |
| Transport | 4 Transport | TCP, UDP |
| Internet | 3 Network | IP, ICMP |
| Link | 2 Data Link, 1 Physical | Ethernet, Wi-Fi |

**How to decide which to use in an answer:** default to TCP/IP for anything about how the real internet works; reach for OSI only when you need to name a specific sub-concern precisely (e.g. "that's a presentation-layer job — encoding, not routing").

Each layer gives its chunk of data a different name — the **Protocol Data Unit (PDU)**:

- **Bits** — physical layer, raw electrical/optical/radio signal
- **Frames** — data link layer, addressed by MAC
- **Packets** — network layer, addressed by IP
- **Segments** (TCP) or **Datagrams** (UDP) — transport layer, addressed by port
- **Data/Message** — application layer

Interviewers use this vocabulary precisely: saying "the packet was dropped" when you mean a frame (a switch, not a router, dropped it) signals you don't actually track which layer did what.

Sending an HTTP request, each layer wraps the layer above's output in its own header, treating everything inside as opaque payload:

![Encapsulation: HTTP data wrapped by TCP, then IP, then Ethernet headers](assets/encapsulation-flow.svg)

By the time it hits the wire, the original HTTP bytes are buried under three headers — and the sending NIC doesn't know or care that there's HTTP inside.

assets.alt: Encapsulation: HTTP data wrapped by TCP, then IP, then Ethernet headers

slides.markdown:
The receiving host runs encapsulation **in reverse**: the NIC strips the Ethernet header and hands the packet up to IP; IP strips its header and hands the segment up to TCP; TCP strips its header and hands the raw bytes up to the application.

Each layer only reads its own header, then passes the remaining payload up unopened — it has no idea what's inside beyond that. This is the same interface discipline that made layering useful in the first place: the IP layer never parses HTTP, and never needs to.

slides.sectionTitle: OSI is a model, not a machine
slides.subTitle: "Where does OSI actually run?" — nowhere, literally
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is treating OSI as something a real machine literally implements layer-by-layer in separate modules. It isn't — no OS ships a "Presentation layer" process. OSI is a **conceptual reference model** used to reason about and teach networking; the software that actually moves your bytes is organized around TCP/IP's four layers.

When an interviewer asks "which OSI layer does X live at," they're testing whether you can classify a *responsibility* (encryption, routing, framing) — not asking you to find a literal OSI module in the Linux kernel.
